blocks.text: The announcement in verses 7-12 belongs to Isaiah 40-55's larger portrayal of comfort and return from Babylon. Creation and exodus imagery present this return as a new homecoming, while not suggesting that the wounds of displacement or later conflicts simply disappeared. The beautiful feet in verse 7 belong to the messenger who announces that decisive good news. Romans 10:15 most directly cites this verse; Nahum 1:15 offers a related messenger parallel but is not Paul's direct source.

Isaiah 52:13 begins a servant passage that continues through Isaiah 53:12. It moves through the servant's humiliation, suffering, death, representative bearing, vindication, and benefit to others, yet it never explicitly names him. Collective, individual, prophetic, messianic, and christological identifications therefore represent different interpretive histories rather than a name supplied by the passage itself.

The wording and reception of this servant passage have a complex textual history. Old Greek Esaias is an ancient Jewish translation and interpretation; some differences may reflect a different Hebrew Vorlage—an underlying Hebrew text—while others may arise from the translator's linguistic or theological choices. The nearly complete Great Isaiah Scroll broadly agrees with the Masoretic tradition but also contains many spelling and substantive differences, and other Qumran manuscripts show continued transmission and interpretation. These witnesses should be distinguished from later questions about prediction, typology, quotation, allusion, Jewish reception, and christological or ecclesial readings.
